newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu meets PLO security officials on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu meets PLO security officials on Hebron.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Palestinian security officials on Friday as peace teams pressed ahead with efforts to close a deal on a long-overdue Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, officials said.

Palestinian West Bank Preventive Security Chief Jibril Rajoub said the session had paved the way for top-level meetings between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Netanyahu and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.
"I believe we are very close to completing the agreement," Rajoub told reporters. "The subjects of contention are limited."
Rajoub said Arafat would meet Mordechai on Sunday and later with Netanyahu, but did not specify exactly when.
The sides discussed the details of security arrangements that will govern Hebron after the handover of 80 percent of the West Bank town to PLO self-rule, officials on both sides said.
"The Prime Minister said during the meeting that he is standing firm concerning the security requirements of Israel in Hebron," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

The statement said Netanyahu spoke with Arafat by telephone at the behest of the Palestinian team during the meeting. Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh declined comment on when Netanyahu would hold a future meeting with Arafat.

Hebron itself remained tense on Friday as three petrol bombs were thrown at an Israeli army observation post near a Jewish settler enclave in the heart of the city holy to Moslems and Jews and a bastion of militancy for both.
The incident occurred shortly after Netanyahu aide and key negotiator Yitzhak Molho toured Hebron, home to 400 Jews and more than 100,000 Palestinians.
Witnesses said Israeli soldiers rounded up and later released about two dozen Palestinians who were in the area. They said the soldiers smelled the men's hands for signs of petrol.
Jewish settlers began hurling rubbish from their enclave at Palestinians after the petrol bombs were thrown. Witnesses said Israeli troops quickly intervened to stop them.
The incident was the latest in a series of attacks in Hebron since U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross broke a three month deadlock in the talks during a peace shuttle last week.
Ross, who nudged Netanyahu and Arafat together in a meeting on Tuesday, was due back in the Middle East on Monday.

Palestinian negotiators said that the breakthrough came when Israel agreed to adhere to the original text of the deal. But Israeli officials insist the accord now being drafted provides better security for Jewish settlers in Hebron.

Hebron is the last of seven West Bank cities occupied since the 1967 Middle East war that Israel agreed to turn over to the Palestinian Authority under a 1995 self-rule deal signed by the previous left-leaning government.
Arafat told Palestinian lawmakers at a closed session on Thursday that he expected the Hebron accord to be ready for signing by December 30 or 31, the deputies said.
Mordechai said in an interview published on Friday that holding up the deal in order to gain more concessions from the Palestinians could risk igniting the whole region.

"Maybe we could have obtained more in one corner or another but that is the nature of negotiations. And today, because of some dump in Hebron we'll ignite the whole region?" Maariv newspaper quoted Mordechai as saying.
